46.title: Bytecode Breadcrumbs
46.description:
A tiny synthetic decoder applies three operations to each byte. Trace the code; do not execute unknown binaries. Recover the UTF-8 training token and submit it exactly.

```python
def decode(hex_text):
 out = bytearray()
 for i, value in enumerate(bytes.fromhex(hex_text)):
 value ^= 0x31
 value = (value - 3 * i) & 0xff
 value = ((value >> 1) | ((value & 1) << 7)) & 0xff # rotate right by 1
 out.append(value)
 return out.decode("utf-8")
```

66.title: Loop Logic
66.description:
A fictional licensing tool hides its activation string with this routine. You have the source and the encoded output; the original is the flag.

```python
KEY  = [199, 124, 17, 97]
SEED = 131

def encode(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    out, acc = [], SEED
    for i, ch in enumerate(data):
        v = (ch + KEY[i % len(KEY)] + acc) & 0xFF
        v ^= (i * 7 + 3) & 0xFF
        out.append(v)
        acc = (acc + ch) & 0xFF      # accumulates the PLAINTEXT byte
    return bytes(out)
```

Encoded output (hex):

```text
9c9d7e22131619c082e027a0defe0e4ccbab16ec
```

Reverse the routine and submit the original string.

100.description:

```pseudo
for i in 0..n-1:
    v = KEY[i]
    v = (v * M[i]) mod 256      ; MUL  (M[i] is always odd)
    v = (v + C[i]) mod 256      ; ADD
    if v != TARGET[i]: fail
```

The per-position constants, read from the binary, are below.

```text
i    M     C     TARGET
0    39    129   23
1    117   128   169
2    41    48    206
3    101   86    195
4    79    250   198
5    63    246   142
```

Every `M[i]` is odd, so each step is invertible modulo 256. Recover `KEY[i]` for every position, decode as ASCII, and submit `UCC{key}`.

Reassemble the data in order (de-duplicate retransmissions). It is Base32 (case-insensitive, padding removed). Submit the decoded flag exactly as recovered.

76.title: Handshake Stories
76.description:
Submit the `UCC{...}` value you recover.

**Scenario.** A field unit authenticates with a PIN-keyed challenge-response handshake. A packet capture from an earlier session was left on the server. Understand the protocol, then authenticate as `ops`.

98.title: Fragmented Trail
98.description:
A capture recorded two interleaved TCP streams out of arrival order, with some segments retransmitted (logged twice, identical sequence number and payload). Reassembly must go by **sequence number**, not log order, and duplicate (seq, payload) pairs should only be counted once.

```text
stream              seq   payload_hex
stream-3c98         1360  6572
stream-0fab         2181  ea88
stream-0fab         2174  cac6
stream-3c98         1360  6572
stream-3c98         1360  6572
stream-3c98         1355  676c
stream-0fab         2179  0d3e
stream-0fab         2176  d82cec
stream-3c98         1357  616369
stream-0fab         2183  8a
```

Isolate the one stream that carries a readable word, reassemble its payload bytes in sequence-number order (deduplicating retransmissions), decode as ASCII, and submit `UCC{word}`.

50.title: Bucket Boundary
50.description:
A fictional training account contains three role policies. Identify the role whose statement permits every object action across every bucket path. Submit `UCC{role_name}` with underscores instead of hyphens.

```json
[
  {"role":"course-reader","effect":"Allow","action":["object:GetObject"],"resource":"bucket/course-materials/lesson/*"},
  {"role":"report-builder","effect":"Allow","action":["object:ListBucket","object:GetObject"],"resource":"bucket/weekly-reports/*"},
  {"role":"emergency-restore","effect":"Allow","action":["object:*"],"resource":"bucket/*/*"}
]
```

Compare both action breadth and resource breadth. This is a static synthetic review; no cloud account is accessed. [Review the cloud path](/training-cloud-security).

61.title: Public by Mistake

69.title: Wildcard Policy
69.description:
Fictional cloud IAM evaluation: an **explicit Deny always wins**, otherwise any matching Allow grants access; default is deny. `*` in an action or resource matches any characters. A principal's effective statements come from its own policies **and** from every group it belongs to.

Policy ReadOnly
```json
[
 {
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
   "s3:Get*",
   "s3:List*"
  ],
  "Resource": "*"
 }
]
```

Policy BuildBuckets
```json
[
 {
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::cs-build-*"
 }
]
```

Policy OpsWide
```json
[
 {
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": "*"
 },
 {
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": "s3:Delete*",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::cs-audit-logs/*"
 }
]
```

Policy OldArchive
```json
[
 {
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:Delete*",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::cs-audit-logs/2025/*"
 }
]
```

Policy Archivers
```json
[
 {
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:Delete*",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::cs-audit-logs/2026/*"
 }
]
```

Principals and groups:

```text
hawa: policies=- groups=Archivers
yusuf: policies=ReadOnly groups=-
mercy: policies=BuildBuckets groups=-
tendo: policies=OpsWide groups=Archivers
samuel: policies=OldArchive groups=-
peter: policies=ReadOnly groups=BuildTeam
group Archivers: policies=Archivers
group BuildTeam: policies=BuildBuckets
```

Exactly one principal can perform `s3:DeleteObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::cs-audit-logs/2026/q3.log`. Submit `UCC{principal}`.

77.title: Role Chain
77.description:
Submit the `UCC{...}` value you recover.

**Scenario.** A fictional CI runner has a cloud identity. A metadata service, a token service and object storage are exposed. The report you need is stored where the runner cannot read it directly. Find a path of allowed role switches.

96.title: Trust Chain Break
96.description:
A fictional cloud account's roles each have a trust policy: a list of `Allow`/`Deny` entries naming which other role may assume them. Matching uses shell-style wildcards (`*`). **An explicit `Deny` always overrides any `Allow` for that same (source, role) pair**, exactly like real IAM evaluation -- it does not matter how many `Allow` entries also match.

```text
Allow edge-ingest      -> relay-worker
Allow metrics-agent    -> audit-reader
Allow edge-ingest      -> audit-reader
Allow relay-*          -> audit-reader
Allow relay-worker     -> ops-admin
Allow metrics-agent    -> backup-svc
Allow metrics-agent    -> backup-svc
Allow audit-reader     -> backup-svc
Deny  backup-svc       -> metrics-agent
Deny  backup-svc       -> metrics-agent
Deny  edge-ingest      -> vault-keeper
Allow ops-admin        -> vault-keeper
```

Starting from `edge-ingest`, find the one chain of role-assumptions (each hop allowed and not denied) that reaches `vault-keeper`. Submit `UCC{role1_role2_role3_role4}` using every role name on the path, in order, joined by underscores.

51.title: Lantern Ledger
51.description:
A fictional public event has two conflicting venue notices. Use source date, authority, and provenance to find the current venue. Submit `UCC{venue_words}` with spaces replaced by underscores. All sources and names below are fabricated for this exercise.

```text
SOURCE A — event page, official.example.training/events/lantern
Updated: 12 Sep 2026 14:20 EAT
Notice: CS26-17 (linked correction)
Current venue: Training Annex East

SOURCE B — poster v1, published 10 Sep 2026
Venue: Training Annex West
Version: superseded

SOURCE C — repost, 12 Sep 2026
Copies poster v1; no source link or correction notice
```

Cite the source and date that resolve the conflict. Do not search for or identify real people. [Review the OSINT path](/training-osint).

62.title: Badge Lookup
62.description:
A public photo caption helps you identify an employee of a fictional company from its staff directory. Use only what the post says.

```text
Post, fictional social network, 2026-09-18: "Quiet morning on the 1st floor. Our Finance team is the only one up here, and my lanyard badge ends in 23."
```

Staff directory:

```text
id        name               dept         floor
EMP-4016  Felix Mugisha      Engineering  1
EMP-7034  Joel Nabirye       Operations   2
EMP-6123  Felix Achieng      Finance      1
EMP-8426  Amina Achieng      Finance      2
EMP-5762  Karen Mugisha      Security     2
EMP-9761  Cynthia Kato       Finance      2
EMP-7240  Karen Nabirye      Operations   5
EMP-1977  Brian Nabirye      Operations   3
EMP-6033  Louis Atim         Legal        3
EMP-2297  Irene Nabirye      Finance      4
```

Submit `UCC{employee_id}` in lowercase, with the hyphen changed to an underscore.

70.title: Handle Hunt

72.title: Source Check
72.description:
A fictional claim is spreading and you must find where it **really** came from. Each article states whether it is based on a primary document or relays another article (`via`). Republished or updated timestamps do **not** change the origin.

```text
A388 | Campus Pulse   | published 2026-10-13 12:24 | updated 12:24 | source: via A795
A500 | Rift Report    | published 2026-10-13 13:06 | updated 13:06 | source: via A698
A299 | Pearl Wire     | published 2026-10-13 09:00 | updated 12:50 | source: PRIMARY (court filing 2026-0412)
A113 | Source Desk    | published 2026-10-13 11:15 | updated 11:15 | source: via A388
A698 | Daily Lantern  | published 2026-10-13 17:17 | updated 17:17 | source: via A500
A795 | Nile Courier   | published 2026-10-13 09:56 | updated 09:56 | source: via A907
A409 | Metro Brief    | published 2026-10-13 13:03 | updated 13:03 | source: via A907
A907 | Savannah Post  | published 2026-10-13 09:53 | updated 15:08 | source: via A299
```

Starting from article **A388**, follow the `via` links until you reach the article that cites a primary document. Submit `UCC{article_id}` of that origin article.

99.title: Chain of Custody

87.title: Welcome Aboard
87.description:
UCC Cyber Stars runs its live announcements, outages, and participant support on Discord, not just this portal. Join the official server: **https://discord.gg/XX28BhvR3**

The flag for this challenge is pinned in the **#start-here** channel (also shown in the channel topic). It is not anywhere on this site.

This one is free. Keep direct messages about other challenges' flags or solutions out of the server — that is still a rules violation even here.

hints.content: Pinned messages in #start-here, and the channel topic line.

78.title: Triage Queue
78.description:
You are the on-call analyst at a fictional regional telecom. The SIEM exported four days of alerts. The queue is noisy, and automation has already flagged several four-step sequences that look like intrusions: **repeated failed logins, a successful login from the same address, an encoded command, then a large transfer to an unusual destination.**

Only one of them is a real compromise. The others are explained by infrastructure in the asset inventory.

Files: `alerts.csv` (2,872 alerts) and `assets.csv` (known infrastructure).

Find the real intrusion and submit `UCC{alert_id}` for its **first** alert (the first failed-login alert from the attacking address), lowercase, with the hyphen changed to an underscore (for example `UCC{a_000123}`).

79.title: Slow Burn
79.description:
A fictional operator's customer portal sits behind nginx. Three days of its access log (about 28,337 requests) are attached (`access.log.gz`, standard *combined* format, timestamps in **local time, UTC+3**). Security later learned that a database backup was downloaded by someone who should not have been able to read it.

The log contains crawlers, uptime monitors, automated internet scanners, ordinary customers, and a legitimate nightly backup job that authenticates with HTTP basic auth. Most scanners are loud. The person you want is not.

Identify the address that downloaded the backup **without authenticating**, then find when that address **first appears in the log**.

Submit `UCC{ip_HHMMSS}` with the dots in the address changed to underscores and the time in **UTC** (24-hour, no separators), for example `UCC{203_0_113_9_142530}`.

80.title: Beacon Hunt
80.description:
Threat intelligence says an implant on your fictional network is calling home on a timer with **random jitter**. Two Zeek logs from the internal sensor cover 36 hours: `conn.log.gz` (about 192,287 connections) and `dns.log.gz`.

Things that look suspicious but are not: strictly periodic services (monitoring, time sync, update checks), and at least one chatty keep-alive to a very popular destination that many hosts also use. The implant's destination is rare: **only one internal host talks to it.**

Identify the **internal host**, the **destination IP** and the beacon's **typical interval in seconds** (the median time between its connections, rounded to a whole second).

Submit `UCC{host_destination_interval}` with the dots in both addresses changed to underscores (for example `UCC{10_0_0_5_203_0_113_9_300}`).

81.title: Triage Console
81.description:
Submit the `UCC{...}` value you recover.

**Scenario.** You are on call at a fictional operator. Your instance is a mini-SIEM holding three days of telemetry (logons, web proxy, endpoint, firewall and DNS) with **one real intrusion** hidden among look-alikes: benign automation, blocked phishing attempts and expected backups. The delivery method is different on every instance. Read the console's help page, reconstruct the incident, and file the six findings. Mind the time zones. Searches are rate-limited, so hunt with intent.

97.title: Lateral Movement
97.description:
A fictional SOC's process-execution log is below, covering three independent process trees across three workstations. Known-good outbound destinations (already resolved and approved) are: `backup-sync.internal, update-relay.internal, metrics-collector.internal`. Every other outbound destination is unresolved and must be treated as suspicious.

```text
event  host    process          parent  dst
e11    WKS-19  explorer.exe     e10     backup-sync.internal
e9     WKS-19  explorer.exe     e8      backup-sync.internal
e10    WKS-19  conhost.exe      e9      update-relay.internal
e3     WKS-07  powershell.exe   e2      -
e4     WKS-07  rundll32.exe     e3      backup-sync.internal
e8     WKS-19  winword.exe      -       -
e1     WKS-07  powershell.exe   -       -
e7     WKS-12  svchost.exe      e6      beacon-drop-05.ext
e2     WKS-07  backup-agent.exe e1      -
e5     WKS-12  explorer.exe     -       -
e6     WKS-12  outlook.exe      e5      -
```

Follow the `parent` links to reconstruct each tree. Exactly one tree's final (leaf) event connects to a destination that is **not** on the allowlist -- that is the real lateral-movement chain. Submit `UCC{destination}` using that one unresolved destination exactly as logged.

82.title: Manifest Reader
82.description:
A field-operations app from a fictional operator is about to ship. Security review has the signed release build (`fieldops-release.apk`). It declares several **content providers**: some are private, some are protected by a permission, and **one can be read by any other app installed on the same phone without asking for anything.**

Inspect the app's manifest (tools such as `aapt2 dump xmltree`, `apktool` or `jadx` will help; the manifest inside an APK is binary XML). Remember that an exported provider is only protected if a read permission applies to it.

Submit `UCC{authority}` for the unprotected exported provider, in lowercase, with the dots changed to underscores.

83.title: Shared Secrets
83.description:
A fictional operator's staff keep personal notes in an Android app, `vaultnotes.apk`. A phone was seized after an incident and the app's private data directory was imaged as `userdata.tar.gz` (shared preferences, files and SQLite databases, as pulled from `/data/data/`).

The note bodies in the database are encrypted. The app can open them, so everything needed is in the package and the image: but **notes were not all written under the same circumstances**, and the way the app picks its key matters. Work out how the app derives the key and opens a note, then read the notes.

One note holds a recovery code in the usual `UCC{...}` form. Submit it exactly.

84.title: Deep Link Gate
84.description:
A fictional operator sells airtime vouchers. Its Android app, `redeemer-3.4.apk`, redeems an order when opened from a link of the form `ucc://redeem?order=&sig=`. The app rejects links whose signature is wrong, and the signing key is not stored anywhere obvious in the app.

Support needs a valid link for order **ORD-951102**, but the signing service is down. Work out exactly how the app builds and checks signatures (the current scheme, not an older one that is still in the code), and compute the signature for that order.

Submit `UCC{signature}` with the signature exactly as the app would expect it in the link.

85.title: Packed Courier
85.description:
A fictional operator's courier-tracking app, `courier-release.apk`, looks tiny: the visible code only loads something and shows a length. The real logic ships as an **encrypted module** inside the package and is unpacked at runtime. The developers claim it cannot be read unless the APK is the genuine, correctly signed build.

Recover the module and read what it returns. The `UCC{...}` value it holds is your answer; submit it exactly.

You do not need a device. Everything required is inside the APK.

86.title: Bytecode Bazaar
86.description:
A fictional operator licenses its field tool with a 20-character key. The Android build, `bazaar-licence.apk`, does not compare the key to a string. It runs it through a **small virtual machine**: the checking program ships as an encrypted blob, and the interpreter's instruction encoding is private to this build.

The valid key is the inner part of a flag: `UCC{` + 20 characters + `}`. No other input is accepted, and nothing in the package states it outright. Recover the key by understanding the machine and reversing the program it runs, then submit the full flag.

88.title: Flip the Switch
88.description:
A fictional kiosk binary, `flip`, asks for an access code before it will print anything interesting. It is a real, statically-compiled 64-bit ELF (no PIE, no stack protector) -- run it, trace it, or just read it.

`file flip` and a disassembler are enough: there is a guard variable sitting right next to an undersized buffer on the stack. You do not need to find a return address or build a ROP chain for this one -- just overflow the right amount into the right place.

Run it locally (it needs no network, no server) and submit whatever it prints.

89.title: Format Leak
89.description:
A fictional diagnostic tool, `leak`, echoes back whatever you type -- but it hands your input straight to `printf` as the *format string itself*, not as data. That is a real, classic bug class: the flag is sitting somewhere else on this process's stack, and `printf`'s variadic machinery will happily read past its real arguments if you ask it to.

Run the binary locally, feed it format specifiers like `%7$lx`, and scan outward until something looks like flag bytes read in 8-byte little-endian words. You will need more than a handful of positions -- the flag is not adjacent to where your input starts.

Submit the flag you recover.

101.title: Return Policy
101.description:
A fictional kiosk binary, `win`, reads far more input than its buffer can hold and never checks the length. It is a real, statically-compiled 64-bit ELF (no PIE, no stack protector). Somewhere in the binary is a `print_flag` function that normal control flow never calls.

Find the exact offset from the start of the overflowed buffer to the saved return address, find `print_flag`'s address (`nm`/`objdump`/your disassembler of choice), and redirect execution there.

Run it locally (it needs no network, no server) and submit whatever it prints.

102.title: Argument Control
102.description:
A fictional kiosk binary, `win`, has the same unchecked overflow as before, but this time `print_flag` takes a 64-bit argument and only prints if it exactly matches a constant you can read straight out of the disassembly: that constant is `0x97477d`.

A function's return address alone cannot set its arguments -- the x86-64 calling convention passes the first argument in `rdi`. You will need a small chain: something that pops a value into `rdi` and returns, before continuing on to `print_flag`.

Run it locally (it needs no network, no server) and submit whatever it prints.

103.title: Full Control
103.description:
Same unchecked overflow as before, but the flag is split across two gated functions this time: `print_flag_part1` only prints if its argument is `0xb11e91`, and `print_flag_part2` only prints if its argument is `0xafe1c2`. A single ret2win jump calls one function; you need both halves.

After a `pop rdi; ret` gadget loads a value and returns, execution continues to whatever address comes next on the stack -- so the same gadget can be reused for a second call, right after the first one returns.

Run it locally (it needs no network, no server) and submit the two halves joined together, exactly as printed.
